---
title: "Why Sarathy Exists"
---


## The problem, stated honestly {#sec-origin-problem}

Personal AI assistants are, at the time of writing, mostly products rather than
systems. They are large, opinionated, and — for the person actually trying to
understand them — opaque. The author's complaint, recorded in the project README,
is specific and worth quoting as a design constraint rather than as a complaint:

> mainstream open implementations of this category are "heavily bloated and
> impossible for me to understand the data flow"; they "cater to all needs".

That is the whole brief. Two words in it carry the engineering programme:

- **"bloated"** → build only the features actually used, and be able to delete the
  rest without ceremony. Every subsystem must justify its existence.
- **"data flow"** → the operator must be able to trace any message end to end, by
  reading code, without a debugger or an observability stack. Traceability is a
  first-class requirement, not a nice-to-have.

Those two words explain most of what follows in this book. A message bus with two
dataclasses, rather than an event-sourcing framework, exists because the data flow
must be legible. JSONL session files, rather than a document database, exist because
a human must be able to read a conversation with `cat`. A `Tool` ABC with one
`execute()` method, rather than a plugin marketplace, exists because "bloated" is
the failure mode being engineered against.

## The starting point {#sec-origin-fork}

Sarathy is a fork of **nanobot**, an existing minimal Python agent. Two other
projects shaped the direction: **nanoclaw**, which demonstrated that a genuinely
small assistant is enough for daily use, and a public argument for personalizing
agents — assistants tuned to one person rather than to everybody.

Forking rather than starting from zero was a deliberate trade: inherit a working
agent loop, message bus and provider layer, and spend the saved effort on the parts
that are actually personal — memory, channels, sessions, scheduling. The cost of
that trade is now visible in the tree: the fork's shape (bus → loop → tools) is
still the skeleton, and everything distinctive has been grown on top of it.

The name means *helper, guide, driver, mentor* in both Sanskrit and Tamil. It is
chosen to describe the relationship the author wants with the tool: a driver who
holds the map, not an oracle.

## From fork to independent architecture {#sec-origin-evolution}

The fork was a starting point, not a destination. Over 878 commits the package
moved from "nanobot, lightly edited" to a system with subsystems that did not exist
at all in the original:

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-evolution
%%| fig-cap: "Subsystems that exist today and did not exist in the starting fork. Each row is a commit range in the history, not a plan."
flowchart LR
  subgraph fork["The fork, as inherited"]
    F1[bus] --> F2[agent loop] --> F3[tools]
    F1 --> F4[providers]
  end
  subgraph grown["Grown on top, in order"]
    G1[channel adapters] --> G2[session store + archival]
    G2 --> G3[skills + hot reload]
    G3 --> G4[memory + idle-time review]
    G4 --> G5[cron + heartbeat]
    G5 --> G6[web dashboard]
    G6 --> G7[usage telemetry]
    G7 --> G8[backend trigger path]
  end
  F3 --> G1
  F4 --> G7
  style fork fill:#eef2f6,stroke:#8aa0b4
  style grown fill:#eaf3ec,stroke:#5f8a6d
```

Four structural changes mark the transition from "fork" to "architecture":

1. **The gateway.** The assistant stopped being a one-shot CLI and became a
   long-lived daemon (`sarathy/gateway/run.py`) that owns every subsystem in a
   single asyncio process. Lifecycle management (`start`/`stop`/`restart`/
   `status`/`logs`) and log rotation came with it
   (`sarathy/gateway/manager.py`).
2. **Channels as adapters.** Telegram, Discord, Email, a web dashboard and — since
   0.15.0 — a localhost-only backend trigger path all implement one interface
   (`sarathy/channels/base.py`) and speak two dataclasses. The agent stopped
   knowing which chat platform it was talking to.
3. **Sessions became a subsystem.** Append-only JSONL transcripts with a metadata
   header line, an LRU cache in front, a SQLite index beside them, and explicit
   archival with a verification stamp (`sarathy/session/manager.py`).
4. **Learning became a pipeline.** Memory writes used to race with each other from
   three different call sites; they are now produced by a single idle-time
   reviewer that refuses to run while the main model is busy
   (`sarathy/session/review.py`).

Each of those is documented in [Chapter 2](02-architecture.qmd); the reasoning
behind them is in [Chapter 4](04-decisions.qmd).

## What "local-first" means here, concretely {#sec-origin-local-first}

"Local-first" is usually a slogan. In this repository it is a specific, checkable
set of commitments:

- **Local models are the default, not a fallback.** The default model in
  `sarathy/config/schema.py` is a local Ollama model; the provider registry
  (`sarathy/providers/registry.py`) carries exactly four kinds — Ollama, LMStudio,
  vLLM, and "any OpenAI-compatible endpoint" — and three of the four are local by
  construction.
- **No mandatory cloud service.** There is no account, no signup, no hosted
  component in the happy path. Web search and speech-to-text have optional hosted
  providers behind configuration keys, and the assistant degrades cleanly when they
  are absent (`sarathy/providers/transcription.py` logs a warning and returns an
  empty transcript rather than failing).
- **One machine.** The gateway, the database, the model server and the dashboard
  all live on the same host. The only inbound socket bound to anything other than
  loopback is the dashboard, and it is explicitly a LAN-reachable web UI with
  pairing-key authentication (`sarathy/channels/dashboard/server.py`).
- **Plain files as the substrate.** Sessions, memory, skills, cron definitions and
  templates are all files you can open in an editor. SQLite appears only where a
  query surface genuinely earns it: the sessions index, the usage ledger, and the
  jobs ledger that the dashboard reads.
- **Stdlib-first Python.** Requires Python 3.11+, ships as a single wheel, and leans
  on the standard library (`asyncio`, `sqlite3`, `dataclasses`, `argparse`-era
  `pathlib`) for the architecture; third-party libraries are used at the edges
  where they earn their place (LLM transport, chat-platform APIs, HTTP).

## What this project is not {#sec-origin-scope}

Stated up front so the book is not read as a framework recommendation:

- **It is not a general-purpose framework.** The README says so explicitly and
  declines feature requests and pull requests; the project exists as a working
  personal assistant that happens to be public.
- **It is not a research artifact.** There are no benchmarks, no eval harness, no
  model comparisons. The success criterion is "the assistant works every day".
- **It is not multi-tenant.** Session keys are scoped to one operator's channels.
  There is no concept of two users sharing a gateway.
- **It is not a place for secrets.** Credentials live in the operator's own config
  file, are never written to sessions, and are redacted before any config value is
  handed back over the dashboard API (`redact_config` in
  `sarathy/channels/dashboard/auth.py`).
